 Rural Minnesota Seniors Could Pay Thousands More as Medicare Advantage Plans Disappear in 2027
 Published Nov 15, 2026 10:28 AM EST 
 By
 Elena Vega 
 Joe Raedle | Getty Images 
 Share on Twitter 
 Share on Facebook 
 Share on WhatsApp 
 Seniors in three Minnesota counties will have no Medicare Advantage plans to choose from in 2027, and some are finding that the replacements cost far more. Steve Myhro, 71, of Nisswa in Crow Wing County, estimates his household's costs could rise by as much as $7,000 a year, MPR News reported Nov. 13.
 Myhro and his wife, Sarah, paid about $2,900 a year for their Blue Cross and Blue Shield of Minnesota Medicare Advantage plan. Their replacement, a Medigap policy plus a separate prescription drug plan , will cost more than $9,000 a year.
 Myhro's example is one household, not a statewide average. But it shows the choice facing many older adults on fixed incomes in rural counties, where the low-premium plans they relied on are disappearing with less than a month left to choose.
 Three Counties Lose Every Medicare Advantage Plan
 Crow Wing, Wadena and Lake of the Woods counties will have no Medicare Advantage plans available in 2027. Fifteen more counties will also lose these plans, though Medicare cost plans and original Medicare remain available there.
 This is the second year in a row that many Minnesota seniors have had to rethink coverage. Last fall, UCare's closure forced more than 150,000 people to find new coverage.
 Statewide, nearly 390,000 Minnesotans received notices in October that their Medicare Advantage plans would be discontinued next year, MPR News reported last month.
 More Minnesotans are losing their Medicare Advantage plans for 2027 than residents of any other state, according to a Star Tribune analysis . Humana is ending individual Medicare Advantage plans in Minnesota, while Blue Cross and Blue Shield of Minnesota is restructuring its plans so substantially that Medicare rules require discontinuing existing ones and offering new ones.
 Nationally, about 4.3 million Medicare beneficiaries will have a Medicare Advantage or stand-alone drug plan terminated at the end of 2026, according to KFF .
 The Price of Switching to Medigap
 For seniors in counties without Medicare Advantage, the main alternative is original Medicare plus a Medigap supplement and a separate Part D drug plan. That combination usually has higher monthly premiums but lower costs when people use care.
 Nicole Converse, a broker at RG Insurance in Baxter, said Medicare Advantage premiums previously ranged from $0 to about $120 a month, while comprehensive alternatives can exceed $400 a month. Wadena County residents, many of whom rely mainly on Social Security, are especially affected, she said.
 The burden is heaviest for people with modest fixed incomes who do not qualify for Medicaid or other help. For them, a premium increase of a few hundred dollars a month can compete directly with rent, groceries, and heating bills during a Minnesota winter.
 Insurers Point to Rising Costs and Thin Rural Networks
 Insurers say rising medical and pharmacy costs have produced losses. "In just the past three years, our company has lost more than $500 million on Medicare alone," Blue Cross and Blue Shield of Minnesota CEO Dana Erickson said in October.
 Rural counties are harder to serve. Insurers cite difficulty maintaining provider networks where there are fewer doctors and hospitals.
 Elected officials have taken notice. Myhro wrote to U.S. Rep. Pete Stauber and Gov. Tim Walz, telling them, "We feel blindsided." Stauber said he is reviewing the concerns and is committed to finding practical solutions. Walz's office pointed to state affordability efforts and suggested Myhro contact state legislators.
 Seniors Have Until Dec. 7 to Choose
 Medicare's annual open enrollment period ends Dec. 7. Seniors whose plans are ending should compare options now rather than wait, since brokers and counselors are in high demand.
 People whose Medicare Advantage plan is terminated qualify for a special enrollment period to buy a Medigap policy with guaranteed issue rights, meaning insurers cannot deny coverage or charge more because of a pre-existing condition, according to KFF. Enrollees whose plans are merged into another plan from the same insurer do not get those federal rights.
 Free, unbiased counseling is available through the Minnesota Board on Aging's Senior LinkAge Line and through State Health Insurance Assistance Programs nationwide. Seniors can also compare plans using Medicare's online Plan Finder or by calling 1-800-MEDICARE.
 Before choosing, it helps to list every doctor, hospital, and prescription, then check each against a new plan's network and drug list. Low-income seniors can ask whether they qualify for Extra Help with drug costs or Medicare Savings Programs, which can lower premiums.
 Waiting past Dec. 7 can leave fewer choices. People whose plans are ending can ask a counselor whether a special enrollment period applies to their situation. MedicalDaily will report whether Congress or state officials act on rural Medicare Advantage gaps in 2027.

 Key Questions Answered
 Which Minnesota counties will have no Medicare Advantage plans in 2027? Crow Wing, Wadena, and Lake of the Woods. Fifteen more counties will have only cost plans and original Medicare.
 How many Minnesotans are losing their plans? Nearly 390,000 received notices in October that their Medicare Advantage plans would be discontinued.
 How much more could replacement coverage cost? It varies. One Crow Wing County couple expects costs to rise from about $2,900 to more than $9,000 a year.
 Why are insurers leaving? Insurers cite rising medical and drug costs, financial losses, and difficulty maintaining rural provider networks.
 What is the deadline to choose a new plan? Medicare open enrollment ends Dec. 7.
 Where can seniors get free help? The Senior LinkAge Line, State Health Insurance Assistance Programs, Medicare's Plan Finder, and 1-800-MEDICARE.
